power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Despite being hailed as a promising avenue for preventing increasingly prevalent adolescent mental health problems, digital parenting interventions to strengthen adolescent mental well-being remain scarce.

How such interventions are developed and experienced by end-users provides key insights for their later implementation and contextualizes information on their effectiveness, yet little systemic evidence is available.
Objective: To inform optimal development and aid careful evaluation of digital parenting interventions, this preregistered multimethod study served three aims.

First, to identify theoretical, functional, and user-derived lessons for digital parenting interventions for adolescent mental well-being, distilled from the challenges of developing a novel digital parenting intervention.
Second, to examine user experience in terms of feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness as early markers of implementation success.

Third, to understand whether user experience is linked to characteristics of the intervention (i.e., universal versus personalized delivery), parents (e.g., openness to advice), or adolescents (e.g., depressive symptoms).

Methods: Development of the intervention was based on Self-Determination Theory and followed an iterative process, including focus groups with parents and adolescents, a pilot study among n = 12 families and subsequent exit-interviews, and a brainstorm session with experts (n = 6).

The intervention was evaluated among parents (N = 199, Mage = 47.6, SDage = 4.7), resulting in administrative and daily diary data of user experience (feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness).
Baseline data were used to test whether intervention, parent, and adolescent characteristics related to user experience.

Results: Findings suggest that adolescent perspectives align with the tenets of selfdetermination theory as a framework that can be translated to concrete advice for parents, that the frequency and delivery of advice should fit family routines, and parental agency and choice were important user needs.

Feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness were sufficient according to our preregistered criteria, but there was substantial heterogeneity between parents and within parents (across days).
User experience did not differ between a personalized and universal version of the intervention.
Parents who were generally more open to advice, and parents of boys, younger adolescents, and less depressed adolescents evaluated the intervention more favorably.

Conclusions: Findings suggest that the fit between our intervention and parents differed substantially across parents, and from tip tot tip, highlighting the need for further refinement of our digital parenting interventions before implementation, and the consideration of user experience throughout development.

text.text: The content of the PARADOx intervention is grounded in applications of Self-Determination Theory (SDT; [32, 33] in the domain of parenting [15, 34, 35].

text.text: This theory forwards three dimensions of parenting that are assumed to feed into adolescents' basic psychological needs for autonomy, relatedness, and competence, namely autonomy support (i.e., promoting volitional functioning), support (e.g., warmth and responsiveness), and structure (e.g., clear boundaries and expectations, process-oriented feedback).

Through fulfilment of adolescents' basic psychological needs, these dimensions of need-supportive parenting are assumed to promote adolescent mental well-being [36, 37], an assumption that has received systematic empirical support (e.g., [38] [39] [40]).

text.text: The PARADOx intervention is fully digitally delivered, without professional blended care, and co-designed with researchers, parents and adolescents, which may strengthen theoretical grounding and ecological fit (i.e., meeting the end-users needs; [41]).

text.text: The intervention includes two elements: a one-time data-driven parent feedback report followed by brief, digital parenting advice formulated as text-based 5-minute challenges and activities.
Challenges were distributed three times per week for six weeks (18 in total; total time investment approximately 1.5 hours).
Two different versions of the intervention were developed that differ in terms of delivery.
In a personalized condition, participants received feedback on their own data and they could choose between several challenges.
In a universal condition, parents received a report based on "the average" parent in the sample and expertselected tips.

Compared to current digital parenting interventions which aim to support adolescent mental well-being, the PARADOx intervention requires a lower time commitment per module, which enhances its scalability.
It also allows comparing personalization in terms of parental agency in choosing between tips with universal advice, and comprehensively examines user experience among a large sample.
For an overview of intervention and study characteristics, see Appendix 1.

Intervention development often remains somewhat of a "black box", potentially leading researchers to continually encounter similar conceptual and practical challenges, rather than building upon a cumulative body of knowledge.

Despite the existence of several frameworks for coding and guiding the development and evaluation of interventions (e.g., [42] [43] [44]), the development process of interventions or lessons which may be derived from it, are still rarely reported [45].

text.text: To further aid the development and careful evaluation of digital parenting interventions, we draw transferable lessons from the development process of the PARADOx intervention.

To integrate and understand the unique interplay between scientific theory and a validated evidence-base and design-related considerations, we developed the intervention in co-creation with end-users during iterative phases, following good practices of the Bloombox Toolkit (https://bloombox.tools/; [46]).

text.text: By iteratively combining insights from scientific theory and evidence-base, parents and adolescents (the direct and indirect end-users), and theoretical experts, we identified three broad lessons derived from challenges encountered during development: (1) theoretical lessons, especially concerning the translation of theoretical principles into concrete intervention content that could be applied in daily life, (2) user-based lessons, which may shape parents' satisfaction and usage of the intervention, including agency and motivation, and (3) functional lessons: technical and practical needs for intervention delivery.
We report parent-, adolescent-, and expert-insights obtained throughout development within these lessons.
A theoretically sound, iteratively designed intervention may still fail however, when intended end users do not (want to) use it in practice [23].
text.formatted: A theoretically sound, iteratively designed intervention may still fail however, when intended end users do not (want to) use it in practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Even when an intervention is distributed at large scale it may yield null results, either because the intervention itself failed to produce such effects, or because users were unsatisfied with how an intervention was delivered and did not apply provided insights.
Without understanding how end-users experienced an intervention, it is therefore hard to grasp and interpret any study on the effectiveness of interventions.

The scarce studies on digital parenting interventions for adolescent mental well-being already provide the very first insights into parents' user experience, focusing mainly on intervention completion [18, 20], or general satisfaction [18].

text.text: While parental satisfaction was generally high (4.29/5; [18]) and feasibility, in terms of program completion, was reasonably strong [18, 21], it remains unknown which specific aspects of the interventions were evaluated more or less favorably, or how they were experienced by parents at all.

text.text: In this study we draw on the Taxonomy of Implementation Outcomes [23, 24] to structurally investigate parents' user experience in an early phase as preconditions for successful implementation, focusing on: (1) feasibility, (2) adoption, (3) acceptability, and (4) appropriateness, as each of these steps are essential to guarantee implementation success at large.

text.text: Feasibility concerns how well an intervention could be applied in its intended setting and population.
We include a single marker of feasibility in terms of compliance, operationalized as the number of tips viewed by parents.
Adoption concerns the (intended) application of insights (i.e., whether parents (intended to) apply provided tips in their daily life).
Acceptability refers to participants' satisfaction with various aspects of an innovation (i.e., perceived helpfulness of tips).
Finally, appropriateness refers to how well an intervention fits, for example, its recipients (i.e., how well parents felt that tips matched their, or their child's needs; [23, 24]).

text.text: Hence, we examine the potential of a personalized version of our intervention compared to a one-size-fits-all version.

text.text: Unfortunately, due to the absence of systematic research on the implementation of digital parenting interventions, it is still unknown for whom interventions are more feasible, which parents are more likely to apply insights, or who might find certain insights most helpful.

Identifying parent and adolescent characteristics which are related to how an intervention was experienced is important both to explain heterogeneity in the effectiveness of parenting interventions and to aid personalization efforts.

Based on scientific literature, we hypothesize that two parent-characteristics in particular are related to the appraisal of a digital parenting intervention: parental openness to advice, and parental perfectionism.
We further explore a range of parent-(e.g., sex, age, baseline parenting practices, parent well-being) and adolescent-characteristics (e.g., sex, age, adolescent well-being).

To address several gaps in research on digital parenting interventions for youth mental health, and to inform the development and implementation of future digital parenting interventions, the current preregistered study (https://tinyurl.com/mrvyn6sf) has three aims.

text.text: First, to structurally describe transferable lessons learned from the development process of the PARADOx intervention.
Second, to describe feasibility and parents' adoption, acceptability and appropriateness as early markers of implementation success.

Third, to understand how these user experience outcomes may depend on intervention, adolescent and parent characteristics, including H1) personalization, H2) parents openness to advice, and H3) parenting perfectionism.
Below, we first describe the iterative development process of the PARADOx parenting intervention from which we draw transferable lessons (Aim 1).
Subsequently, we describe the larger study exploring user experience (Aim 2) and how these outcomes correlate with intervention-specific, parental and adolescent characteristics (Aim 3).

text.text: Parents filled out an online baseline survey (ca. 45 minutes) via Qualtrics to obtain demographic characteristics.
Afterwards, participants received 100 daily surveys (ca. 3-5 minutes) via the Avicenna application on parenting practices and well-being.
To evaluate the intervention, a subgroup of 217 parents received the digital parenting intervention.
Parents received 18 parenting tips over six weeks, embedded within the daily diaries.
User experience outcomes were assessed the day after receiving a tip.
The analytical sample included 199 parents who contributed at least one valid evaluation of a tip.
Data were considered valid if a parent viewed a tip, and subsequently evaluated this tip the following day, resulting in 1963 observations.

Parents (age 36-61 years, Mage = 47.6, SDage = 4.7) were primarily Dutch (95%, 2% European non-Dutch, 3% non-European), biological mothers (82%, 18% biological fathers), and theoretically educated (78% college or university degree, 18% applied education, 4% high-school), living in an urban environment (60%).
Most parents were together with the other biological parent (78%), and either shared parenting responsibilities equally (65%), or considered themselves the primary caregiver (34%).
Mothers were overrepresented, and education level was substantially above the national average [60].

text.text: Feasibility of daily parenting tips was operationalized using administrative data, in terms of the number of daily tips (out of 18) viewed by parents over the course of six weeks.

In daily diaries, parents' evaluation of the adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness was administered through self-reports, via agreement with statements (visual analogue scale from 0 ("Not at all") to 100 ("Very much"), which referred to the tip provided the previous day ("Yesterday, you received a tip.
To what extent do you agree with the following statements about this tip?").
Adoption was measured with a single item ("I applied the tip in my own parenting or intend to do so.").
Acceptability was operationalized with a single item ("I found this tip helpful.").

Appropriateness was operationalized as the average on two items ("The tip suited me well as a parent." and "The tip suited my child well."), which correlated highly with each other across all tips (r = .93).

To allow for qualitative context, parents could share additional thoughts about provided tips ("Would you like to share anything else about the tip?"), which we include to illustrate quantitative findings.

text.text: To build the intervention on a solid theoretical fundament, and to translate a broad theoretical framework into specific parenting practices as intervention targets, we conducted focus groups with adolescents and parents, and iteratively designed and revised parenting tips with theoretical experts and parents.
We identified parenting as a promising context for promoting adolescent mental well-being, identified concrete parenting practices to target, and constructed parenting tips.
"The Home Environment" is Key to Well-Being.
The underlying theoretical assumption that the home environment, parenting specifically, may be a promising target for intervention, was confirmed by adolescents.

A majority (62%) of adolescents in the focus group sessions indicated the home environment, largely because of their parents, as the most important context for their mental well-being, above school, peers, the online domain, or "self" (e.g., personal resilience).

One adolescent (girl, 12 years) illustrated this by highlighting the stable role parents play in their children's lives, when asked whether she felt having arguments with one's parents was "worse" than an argument with friends: "Parents, because you can't get a new parent, but you can get new friends."

To move from broad theoretical dimensions (Self Determination Theory; [32, 33]) to concrete parenting practices for intervention, we qualitatively investigated whether parenting resonated with parents and adolescents as a solution to adolescent mental health problems.
text.formatted: To move from broad theoretical dimensions (Self Determination Theory; <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33]</ref>) to concrete parenting practices for intervention, we qualitatively investigated whether parenting resonated with parents and adolescents as a solution to adolescent mental health problems.

text.text: Adolescents also identified specific parenting practices which they felt were particularly salient to their mental well-being, which aligned with the theoretical needs for parents to promote autonomy (e.g., allowing adolescents room to explore an activity, stepping in with advice afterwards), structure (e.g., establishing clear responsibilities regarding household chores), and relatedness (e.g., taking the time to ask about concrete activities).

For autonomy support, adolescents emphasized that parents should genuinely listen to their perspectives, involve them in decisions affecting them or at least clarify the reasoning behind those decisions, and emphasized the freedom to make mistakes and learn from them.
One adolescent girl (14 years) illustrated the latter: "I think it's good if you also have freedom.

So that your parents are strict, but that at a certain moment they let you discover things for yourself and that they then [afterwards] say, maybe this can be done differently next time and maybe next time we should set our boundaries better, you know like that."
Concerning structure, adolescents considered rules and boundaries as sometimes unpleasant in the immediate moment but important to their well-being in the long term.
One girl (13 years) highlighted the value of predictability that clear rules and boundaries provide: "I find it really convenient if I just know where I stand and what I need to do.
And when someone is going to be home or something like that, so that it's just clear, that nothing ever comes really unexpected or something.
I just know when I have a chore to do, or not."
Finally, concerning relational support, adolescents underlined spending quality time with parents.

One girl (14 years) illustrated this within the context of everyday activities when discussing how parents could best display affection: "Show that they know what you have been doing so then for example ask like 'how did that project end up' or something like that, and then for example with listening just say, like, shall we drink a cup of tea then you can tell me about it', you know, so really making some time, that's nice."
Designing Tips with Experts and Parents.
Throughout development, we constructed the intervention content iteratively with experts, adolescents and parents to optimize the interplay between theoretical validity and ecological fit.
The final tips were rated highly by experts (on average 8.3/10 on theoretical alignment, and 7.7/10 on practicality) and parents (M = 8.5/10 on perceived quality, M = 8.6/10 on practicality).
Whether these scores were equally high in a larger study was tested (see Aim 2) in terms of adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness.

Functional lessons encompass technical or practical insights that may support the delivery or application of parenting interventions and were distilled from (1) the brainstorm session with experts, and (2) the technical pilot study and related semi-structured interviews with parents and adolescents.
We learned that interventions that need to be applied in real life, also need to align with family routines.
That is, delivered at the right frequency (a couple of times per week but not daily), in a format that stimulates activation, combined with attractive and simple data-visualization.
Key to the functional delivery of tips according to parent interviews was that it should align with families' routines.
That is, advice should be delivered in the evenings, outside of the busy daily routine, to aid visibility and application of tips.
Parents also advised that distributing tips daily was considered too much to be able to apply.
Experts mentioned that the form should match the type of provided advice.
For example, if aiming to strengthen a specific skill, advice should promote interactivity with that skill rather than passively presenting theory.

Concerning the intended data-driven personalized feedback report, experts highlighted that visualizations of such complex data should be simple and attractive, which can be facilitated by involving parents throughout the development process.
A second element of our intervention was to apply parenting tips embedded in daily surveys via the Avicenna smartphone application.
Daily surveys in general, collected via the smartphone app during the pilot test, were feasible, with adolescents completing 71.3% of daily surveys during the pilot test, and parents 92.2%.
The feasibility of the study was tested further at larger scale (N = 217, see below).
Throughout development, we identified two important user-derived lessons which may promote satisfaction and usage of digital parenting interventions, namely parental agency, and openness to advice.
Insights were obtained through (1) a brainstorm session with experts, and (2) semi-structured interviews with parents and adolescents following the technical pilot study.
Experts emphasized in a brainstorm session that parents should retain agency by deciding whether they want advice, which advice fits their family, and what advice they choose to apply.

Parents and adolescents likewise indicated such a need for personalization in exit interviews following the pilot study, in that advice should be related to their own parenting, but did highlight an important condition for personalization: privacy.
Parents and adolescents should not have insight into each other's data.
The hypothesis that personalization would lead to better uptake was subsequently tested in the evaluation study (H1).

Parenting advice was generally supported by both parents and adolescents in semi-structured interviews: parents indicated an interest in insight into their family functioning, openness to receiving parenting advice, and positively appraised reflecting on interactions with their child, but some indicated that they would personally experience advice as confronting.
Adolescents were also generally positive about their parents receiving parenting advice, but highlighted that parents should be willing to receive such advice.
The hypothesis that openness is indeed key to user experience was tested in the evaluation study (see Aim 3, H2).
After careful development, the intervention was included in a larger study among 217 parents (with a control group of 314 parents, not included here, but see: [30, 31]).

text.text: Family appropriateness was also modest but generally sufficient (M = 57.5).

Across tips, 68.3% of parents indicated that the tips were a reasonably good fit for themselves and their adolescent (scoring ≥ 50/100), with 21.6% of parents rating tips as ideal (≥ 70/100), and 31.7% rating tips poorly on appropriateness (< 50).

text.text: Despite generally sufficient user experience outcomes, differences in evaluations within parents were pronounced (i.e., how individual parents evaluated specific tips; see Figure 2).

text.text: Qualitative data also illustrate divergent patterns within parents, even within the same parenting domain.

For example: one father (age 53, practically educated) rated a tip on autonomy support about fostering enjoyment of chores insufficient, indicating that the tip did not match their child's age ("I found the tip a little too "childish" and therefore less fitting for a 16-year-old girl.")

However, another tip on autonomy support aimed at creating understanding for family rules, which was delivered later that week, was rated much more positively, being rated as ideal on helpfulness and appropriateness ("Useful tip!
This fosters more understanding when explaining [a rule].").
Offering choice in intervention content may be essential to provide advice, challenges or tips that align well with a family's unique characteristics and momentary circumstances.

Our third aim was to investigate parental, adolescent, and intervention characteristics that might explain differences in user experience.
Three hypotheses were investigated.

First (H1), we expected parents who received the personalized intervention (n = 110), and were offered more choice and agency, to experience the intervention more favorably compared to the universal intervention group (n = 106).

However, no statistically significant differences were identified in feasibility (number of tips viewed; t(206.75) = .31, p = .758), adoption (t(194.25) = .38, p = .708), acceptability (t(189.55) = -.61, p = .541), or family appropriateness (t(192.43) = -1.00, p = .317; see Table 2).

text.text: Hence, personalization did not result in meaningfully different appraisals of intervention content, rejecting H1.

Second, confirming H2, parents who indicated a greater openness to receiving parenting advice at baseline generally experienced parenting tips more favorably across outcomes, which was also identified as a lesson from the development process.

While unrelated to the number of tips viewed (feasibility), openness to advice at baseline was modestly correlated with adoption (r(193) = .27, p < .001), acceptability (r(193) = .20, p = .006), and appropriateness for parent and adolescent (r(193) = .21, p = .004; see Table 4).

Parenting perfectionism was not associated with user experience (see Table 4).

text.text: Concerning parental characteristics, older parents generally viewed slightly more tips (i.e., higher feasibility; r(185) = .15, p = .038).
Baseline parenting practices were also modestly correlated with user experience.

Specifically, more autonomy supportive parents were more likely to (be willing) to apply tips in their own family (r(199) = .14, p = .042), and parents who reported more structure and autonomy support rated the appropriateness of tips for their family higher (respectively: r(199) = .16, p = .028 and r(199) = .16, p = .020).
Parental well-being, self-efficacy, personality, support, and overprotection were not significantly related to user experience.

Adolescent characteristics were unrelated to feasibility, but user experience was generally poorer among parents of older adolescents (adoption: r(199) = -.26, p < .001; acceptability: r(199) = -.18, p = .010; appropriateness: r(199) = -.23, p = .001), and youth with depressive symptoms (acceptability: r(199) = -.14, p = .047; appropriateness: r(199) = -.15, p = .030), and lower for parents of girls (acceptability: r(199) = -.15, p = .031; appropriateness: r(199) = -.14, p = .049).

Parents' qualitative insights also illustrate that the tips were potentially less-suited for older adolescents.

For instance, one mother (age 51, practical education) of a 14-year old girl indicated about a tip promoting enjoyment of household tasks such as cleaning the dishes: "Tips seem intended for younger children, I did this when they were little but they won't fall for this anymore."
Parenting interventions are being hailed as a promising answer to the rising tide of adolescent mental health problems [2, 3, 17].

text.text: Yet despite the established potential of eHealth in other domains, such as to support adolescents' own mental well-being [9], or address children's behavioral problems [25, 29], there are remarkably few scientifically sound digital parenting interventions which directly target parenting to improve adolescents' mental wellbeing [25, 29].

text.text: Although the first evaluations of such interventions in terms of participant engagement and broad indicators of program satisfaction are promising [18, 20, 21], more systematic research programs are needed to guide the optimal development of such interventions and to better understand factors that may facilitate or hinder adequate implementation in practice.

text.text: Therefore, this study on a novel digital parenting intervention (PARADOx) for promoting adolescent mental well-being served three purposes.
First, to describe transferable lessons learned of the development of digital parenting interventions.
From our iterative development process, Self-Determination Theory proved a valuable theoretical framework which could be translated into modifiable parenting targets.
Parental openness to receiving advice, and agency, choice, and privacy in applying advice were key user needs.
Functionally, delivery of advice should align with parents' routines and be unambiguous to promote feasibility.
Second, mapping user experience, parents (N = 225) generally evaluated the intervention sufficiently (scoring ≥ 50/100 on adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness across tips), but not ideal.
There were important individual differences between and within parents in their evaluation of the tips.
Third, we explored parent, adolescent, and intervention characteristics related to parents' user experience.
Personalized advice was not evaluated more favorably compared to universal advice.

Parents who reported a higher openness to advice, and higher autonomy support and structure at baseline generally evaluated tips more favorably, as did parents of boys, parents of younger adolescents, and parents of adolescents with less depressive symptoms.
The development process of our intervention yielded several findings, from which we draw three broad transferable insights concerning future development of digital parenting interventions.

First, a theoretical framework is an important foundation for intervention development, but should be complemented with insights from intended end-users to translate theory into actionable content (see for example Bloombox; https://bloombox.tools/; [46]).
text.formatted: First, a theoretical framework is an important foundation for intervention development, but should be complemented with insights from intended end-users to translate theory into actionable content (see for example Bloombox; <ref type="url" target="https://bloombox.tools/">https://bloombox.tools/</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>).

text.text: Self-Determination Theory proved a particularly useful framework for the development of our digital parenting intervention given its theoretical depth and extensive application to the domain of parenting.
This allowed us to draw from a range of well-described and empirically supported constructs.
However, parent-ratings of the tips during development highlighted that despite a solid theoretical foundation and expert backing, certain tips were found to be poorly applicable in daily life.
This is in line with literature emphasizing the need to include enduser perspectives in the development of parenting programs to improve ecological fit [41].
text.formatted: This is in line with literature emphasizing the need to include enduser perspectives in the development of parenting programs to improve ecological fit <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Second, the success of an intervention depends not solely on the quality of its content: how it is delivered to end-users is equally important, yet a key challenge remains balancing user needs with practical feasibility.
Mapping the needs and preferences of parents can promote their eventual engagement with an intervention providing advice [75].
text.formatted: Mapping the needs and preferences of parents can promote their eventual engagement with an intervention providing advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">[75]</ref>.

text.text: In our qualitative sessions, participants mentioned several needs to improve the end-user experience.
Specifically, advice should be unambiguous, delivered with the right frequency, and the timing of parenting advice should follow family routines.
Crucially, however, such insights do not automatically translate into evident design solutions.
Family routines are not uniform for example, and the optimal timing of advice may differ per family, and even from moment to moment.
Hence, accommodating every preference fully may not be feasible.

The development process of an intervention should extend beyond mapping user needs, also defining which needs can actually be accommodated, to which extent, and how needs are handled that cannot be accommodated.
Third, we suggest a careful balance between providing personalized interventions, and maintaining privacy and agency.

While parents and adolescents felt that advice should meet their personal needs, privacy was also an important condition raised by families; parents and adolescents should not have insight into each other's data.

Parents and adolescents often place great importance om maintaining control over which health related data is shared between them for a variety of reasons [76], and disagreement on such privacy rules may induce conflict [77].
text.formatted: Parents and adolescents often place great importance om maintaining control over which health related data is shared between them for a variety of reasons <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76]</ref>, and disagreement on such privacy rules may induce conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">[77]</ref>.

text.text: This raises an important consideration about how personalization is applied, which is particularly salient to interventions which concern data from multiple sources.

Information which may be of particular use to personalizing advice for one user, may be sensitive information to another user and affect whether a participant feels comfortable engaging with an intervention.
Hence, we suggest that privacy should be viewed not just as a technical or lawful requirement, but as a key condition which may affect how users experience and engage with an intervention.

Given that parents, adolescents, and experts indicated that parental agency in terms of deciding if and how they apply parenting advice was crucial, one solution may be to provide families control over the extent to which their data is used for personalization.

One of the key debates in parenting literature is whether parenting affects adolescent well-being in entirely unique and very diverse ways across families, or whether certain parenting practices are fundamentally beneficial or harmful for all adolescents [78].
text.formatted: One of the key debates in parenting literature is whether parenting affects adolescent well-being in entirely unique and very diverse ways across families, or whether certain parenting practices are fundamentally beneficial or harmful for all adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref>.

text.text: However, even the route towards universally beneficial parenting practices may vary from family to family, and from moment to moment [78].
text.formatted: However, even the route towards universally beneficial parenting practices may vary from family to family, and from moment to moment <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref>.

text.text: Hence, even universally beneficial intervention targets should benefit from personalization by addressing the pathways through which such universal effects are achieved.

Indeed, while parents and adolescents in our study provided various examples of important parenting practices in line with Self-Determination Theory, the exact practices highlighted differed per participant.
Parents and adolescents also indicated that advice should match their own family, and when applied to a larger sample, user experience of tips varied notably between and within families and tips.
That is, most parents evaluated some tips favorably and others poorly, and most tips were rated poorly by some parents, and positively by others.
This would suggest that personalization is needed to align with families' unique circumstances and preferences.

Given the potential benefits of personalization in intervention research [6, 75], and its relevance inferred from our findings, it is surprising that personalization did not result in significantly different appraisals of daily tips in the current study.
text.formatted: Given the potential benefits of personalization in intervention research <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75]</ref>, and its relevance inferred from our findings, it is surprising that personalization did not result in significantly different appraisals of daily tips in the current study.

text.text: This may reflect the rudimentary nature of personalization in our study.

Personalization included parental agency in selecting between different tips within the same theoretical domain, but parents could not choose the domain itself on which they received advice (e.g., advice on providing structure versus autonomy support), and received advice at set times.
This personalization may have been too superficial to really create a sense of agency and ownership among parents.
Personalization may need to be more profound at a content level to account for the uniqueness of parental pathways to universally beneficial practices.

Future studies might investigate other more comprehensive forms of personalization such as allowing parents to choose the very domain on which they receive advice and explicitly exploring different levels of agency, or tailoring advice based on data-driven daily parenting dynamics (i.e., JITAI's; [79]).
text.formatted: Future studies might investigate other more comprehensive forms of personalization such as allowing parents to choose the very domain on which they receive advice and explicitly exploring different levels of agency, or tailoring advice based on data-driven daily parenting dynamics (i.e., JITAI's; <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>).

text.text: More profound tailoring of content has shown potential in strengthening parenting practices [21], but how it affects parents experiences with an intervention remains unknown.
text.formatted: More profound tailoring of content has shown potential in strengthening parenting practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, but how it affects parents experiences with an intervention remains unknown.

text.text: Another reason why personalization may be needed is that the degree to which parents engage in need-supportive parenting fluctuates from day to day [36], depends on their own need-satisfaction [80], and can be driven by adolescents as active agents in the parentchild relationship [50, 81].

text.text: These findings suggest that personalization should concern not just what content is delivered to an individual family, but also when such advice is delivered, and how often it is delivered.

Data-driven algorithms, as used in Just-In-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs; [79]), where the content is adapted to an individual's current (changes in) condition and context, may offer a promising direction for parenting interventions.
text.formatted: Data-driven algorithms, as used in Just-In-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs; <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>), where the content is adapted to an individual's current (changes in) condition and context, may offer a promising direction for parenting interventions.

text.text: It is well-established that parents differ in their openness to be engaged in an intervention, with engagement being critical to effective implementation [83, 84].
text.formatted: It is well-established that parents differ in their openness to be engaged in an intervention, with engagement being critical to effective implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">[83,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">84]</ref>.

text.text: Because the current intervention was developed for a broad target group, we explored characteristics salient to user experience, which may prove vital to further strengthening the intervention before implementation.
We identified three parent characteristics at baseline that were generally associated with more positive user experience: more openness to advice, more structure, and more autonomy support.
The finding that parents who already engage more in the targeted practices or who are more open to advice provided more favorable evaluations, is not inherently problematic.

This pattern does warrant attention however, if poorer evaluation also translates into lower engagement among parents for whom such parenting interventions might be particularly relevant, as the public health benefits of universal prevention rest upon its ability to reach a large population [85].
text.formatted: This pattern does warrant attention however, if poorer evaluation also translates into lower engagement among parents for whom such parenting interventions might be particularly relevant, as the public health benefits of universal prevention rest upon its ability to reach a large population <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">[85]</ref>.

text.text: One way to remedy this problem may be to include explicit motivational strategies, which has shown promise in promoting parental engagement in formal professional interventions [86].
text.formatted: One way to remedy this problem may be to include explicit motivational strategies, which has shown promise in promoting parental engagement in formal professional interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">[86]</ref>.

text.text: Engagement may also be improved by further lowering barriers to entry or increasing perceived relevance, for instance by more comprehensively including parents in the design of a program [75], personalization of intervention features [87], or by tailoring to relevant family characteristics such as cultural needs up front [88].
text.formatted: Engagement may also be improved by further lowering barriers to entry or increasing perceived relevance, for instance by more comprehensively including parents in the design of a program <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">[75]</ref>, personalization of intervention features <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">[87]</ref>, or by tailoring to relevant family characteristics such as cultural needs up front <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">[88]</ref>.

text.text: To increase intervention relevance across the board, it may be particularly salient to include those families in its development who are initially less open or motivated to engage in such an intervention.
By only including highly motivated parents in development efforts, researchers may sustain distance to those who might benefit most.
How an intervention is experienced may depend not only on parents' characteristics, but also on characteristics of their adolescent.
This SDT-based preventive intervention appears to be best experienced by parents of younger adolescents, boys, and parents of adolescents with fewer depressive symptoms.
Limited suitability for parents of older adolescents may reflect a mismatch between intervention content and those families' needs.

An intervention aiming to support parents across adolescence may require substantively different content based on the adolescents' age to align with developmental changes [89], shifting family interactions [90], and resulting needs for advice.
text.formatted: An intervention aiming to support parents across adolescence may require substantively different content based on the adolescents' age to align with developmental changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[89]</ref>, shifting family interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[90]</ref>, and resulting needs for advice.

text.text: Early adolescence may also constitute a time where parents are particularly receptive to advice in general.

Marking the onset of renegotiations of the parent-adolescent relationship, early adolescence is often characterized by increased conflict [91], potentially stemming from discrepancies between parents' and adolescents views of parenting practices [92].
text.formatted: Marking the onset of renegotiations of the parent-adolescent relationship, early adolescence is often characterized by increased conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">[91]</ref>, potentially stemming from discrepancies between parents' and adolescents views of parenting practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">[92]</ref>.

text.text: Because early adolescence in particular may represent a time of profound change in family dynamics, parents may seek additional support and appraise it more positively.
The poorer user experience by parents of adolescents with higher symptoms of depression could be explained through the strain such mental health problems place upon a family.
The Family Adjustment and Adaptation Response (FAAR) Model [93] may (partially) clarify this.
text.formatted: The Family Adjustment and Adaptation Response (FAAR) Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">[93]</ref> may (partially) clarify this.

text.text: Normally, families operate in an equilibrium, with demands upon the family system (e.g., stressors or daily hassles) being balanced out by the family's capabilities (e.g., coping behaviors, resources) to deal with such demands.
However, adolescent symptoms of depression, especially if they persist over an extended period, may constitute an excessive demand upon a family system.
During such a period of disequilibrium, parents may be hampered in their ability to apply parenting advice or even absorb new information.
Alternatively, a family dealing with (increased) symptoms of adolescent depression may simply require more aid than provided via light and universal parenting advice.
Such families may require considerably different help and may benefit more from blended care for example, where digital advice is combined with professionally-guided help (e.g., [27].

text.text: The current study aimed to contribute to better and more systematic procedures to developing digital parenting interventions to support adolescent mental well-being, and provides insight into how parents engage with, and experience such advice.

By extensively investigating parents' user experience with a digital parenting intervention, we provide a systematic overview of factors which may be salient to the development and tailoring of such interventions.
Nevertheless, a number of limitations warrant attention.
First, the generalizability of the current study across countries and socio-economic groups may be limited.
Participants were Dutch families, and parents were primarily highly-educated mothers.
Given that evaluations of parenting interventions may differ depending on cultural considerations [88] and socio-economic factors [87], replication in diverse, cross-national studies is essential.
text.formatted: Given that evaluations of parenting interventions may differ depending on cultural considerations <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">[88]</ref> and socio-economic factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">[87]</ref>, replication in diverse, cross-national studies is essential.

text.text: Second, our intervention was evaluated in a very early stage and thus, we assessed user experience as early pre-implementation indicators (i.e., feasibility, acceptability, adoption, and appropriateness), which should not be confounded with a comprehensive evaluation of a ready-to-implement intervention.

To translate this rudimentary intervention into a real-world setting, requires further iterative development to improve the match between tips and parents' needs [22], and a much more elaborate evaluation (e.g., costs, fidelity, sustainability; [23, 24].

text.text: The current study aimed to identify theoretical, functional, and user-based lessons which may inform the development of digital parenting interventions, and explored how such interventions are evaluated.

Our challenge-based digital parenting intervention was generally evaluated sufficiently well but not ideal, and heterogeneity was considerable: individual parents evaluated different tips very differently, and individual tips were in turn rated differently across parents.
The intervention was evaluated more favorably by parents of younger adolescents and boys, and more poorly for adolescents who reported elevated symptoms of depression.
These findings suggest that the fit between our intervention and parents differs substantially.
To better align intervention content with the needs and preferences of individual families, more comprehensive personalization of intervention (delivery) may be a valuable target for future research.
Focus Groups with Adolescents and Parents.
We conducted focus groups with adolescents and parents to identify parenting behaviors which they felt were most beneficial to adolescent well-being.

Sessions consisted of several steps: after a brief introduction on the topic of the session, participants were asked to freely contribute things they felt affected adolescent mental well-being, which were then grouped into the domain in which they occurred (home, school, friends, self, or online & other).
text.formatted: Sessions consisted of several steps: after a brief introduction on the topic of the session, participants were asked to freely contribute things they felt affected adolescent mental well-being, which were then grouped into the domain in which they occurred (home, school, friends, self, or online & other).

text.text: Subsequently, focus shifted to parenting, with participants generating parenting practices of importance to adolescent mental well-being and grouping them into a quadrant based on whether such practices were "nice" in the moment and/or "good" for adolescent well-being in the long term.
These practices were subsequently rated on importance, and participants considered potential barriers and facilitators for parents to implement promotive practices.
The full protocol for these sessions was preregistered separately (https://tinyurl.com/445xdxev).
text.formatted: The full protocol for these sessions was preregistered separately (<ref type="url" target="https://tinyurl.com/445xdxev">https://tinyurl.com/445xdxev</ref>).

text.text: Between March and April 2024, eight 90-minute sessions were conducted with adolescents aged 12-18 years (N = 57, 70% boys, Mage = 14.6, SDage = 1.6), and two sessions with parents (N = 8, 50% mothers, Mage = 50.8, SDage = 8.7).
Adolescents primarily identified as Dutch (93%), with 20% identifying with at least one (other) non-Dutch culture.
Adolescents mostly lived in an urban (73%) environment.
Participants were recruited via two Dutch high schools offering a variety of educational tracks.
Sessions were conducted by the first author at the participants' school and were audio-and video-recorded and transcribed.

Focus groups resulted in insights into whether parenting as a solution to adolescent mental health problems resonated with adolescents and parents, and which parenting practices might be most salient in this regard, informing promising targets for intervention.

To identify technical needs and (potential) pitfalls on how to translate data into concrete parenting advice, a one-hour brainstorm session was conducted in April 2024 with a panel academic staff (N = 6) from various disciplines, including expertise on e-health and game-design, human-centered design, data-visualization, parenting theory, and parenting intervention design, and randomized controlled trial design.

The parenting intervention was intended to be delivered digitally, in the form of short textbased messages, and therefore we conducted a technical pilot using the intended software platform (Avicenna) for the larger study.

Pilots were conducted with the research team for one week in June 2024 and subsequently for one week with twelve parents (83% mothers; 100% theoretically educated; Mage = 46.6 years, SDage = 3.2) and (one of) their adolescent children (50% girls, 83% theoretically educated, Mage = 14.8 years, SDage = 1.8).

Semistructured exit interviews were conducted with 11 families (one family could not be interviewed) to obtain qualitative insights regarding the desirability of our intended parenting intervention (e.g., "As a parent, would you like to receive parenting advice based on your answers?").

The first element of the intervention, the parenting tips, were developed iteratively.

Based on Self-Determination Theory, tips were aimed at strengthening parental autonomy support, support or structure and were subdivided into 18 dimensions (6 each for structure, autonomy support, and support), each relating to a theoretically important aspect of needsupportive parenting.

Focus groups and expert brainstorms helped the research team (n = 5, Parenting experts) to develop an initial list of 75 tips within this theoretical foundation and were constructed as 5-minute challenges intended to motivate parents to apply new skills or reflect on their parenting.
The initial 75 parenting tips were further refined in three iterative stages between July and August 2024.
First, tips were rated (1-10) by an international panel of theoretical experts (N = 5) on Self-Determination Theory and parenting research, and by parents (N = 4).
Experts rated tips on theoretical quality (How well-supported is this tip by theory on SDT and parenting?), and practicality (How easily might parents implement this in their daily parenting?).
Parents evaluated tips on perceived usefulness (Would a specific tip benefit parents?) and practicality (Can parents implement this in their daily practice?).
Experts and parents could provide open-ended feedback, and experts were free to suggest alternative tips.
Second, we removed tips of insufficient quality (rated < 5.5 by parents or experts, aligning with the Dutch grading system generally qualifying a 5.5 out of 10 as the benchmark for a "pass").

text.text: For the 69 remaining tips, the three highest rated tips (scoring ≥ 7 on average) were selected per parenting dimension, but if tips overlapped significantly in content, selection was based on diversity of content.
Finally, the research team refined the tips on tone (active, clear call to action, nonjudgmental), and language (b1-level appropriate).

Hence, the final tips (1) aligned adequately with Self-Determination Theory, (2) were rated ≥ 7 by experts and by parents on quality and applicability in daily life, and (3) contained appropriate (b1-level) language and tone.
The final version consisted of 53 tips: 18 tips each relating to structure and autonomy support, and 17 tips relating to support (only two tips were maintained for one dimension relating to support).

The second element of the intervention, the one-time parent feedback report, was developed iteratively between June and November 2024 with a designer with experience in designing intervention materials.
